# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel (2026-11-20)

## Short version

jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc 5.3 memory allocator) reduced the p99 latency of kestrel (our key-value store) from 2140 us to 870 us on a read-mostly benchmark; p99 is the time within which 99% of requests finish. Throughput and median latency did not change measurably, but memory use rose by 5.7 GB (9.3%), which the capacity team must approve. Write-heavy load, more than 64 client threads, and NUMA pinning (binding the process to one CPU socket) are not tested yet.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store, the program under test.
- **jemalloc**: an open-source memory allocator library.
- **jf2**: our fork of jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build A**: main@4f1c2aa with jemalloc 5.3.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2.
- **ycsb-b**: workload B of YCSB (Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark), with 95% reads and 5% updates [Ref1].
- **ycsb-a**: workload A of YCSB, with 50% reads and 50% updates [Ref1].
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. A p99 of 870 us means 99% of requests finished in 870 us or less.
- **RSS** (resident set size): the physical memory the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: the jemalloc step that returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **je_arena_decay**: the jemalloc function seen in the profile during the decay purge.
- **perf**: the Linux sampling profiler.

## Test setup

- **Host:** bench-07, 2 x 32-core Xeon (64 cores), 512 GB of memory, kernel 6.8.
- **Load before the runs:** load average 0.4, which means the machine was almost idle.
- **Workload:** ycsb-b with 64 client threads, 10 minutes per run.
- **Runs:** 5 per build, alternating A, B, A, B.
- **Reported values:** the median of the 5 runs, with the lowest and highest run in parentheses.

## Results

```
Latency in us, median of 5 runs. One # = 200 us.

p99    A  ###########  2140
       B  ####  870   59% lower

p99.9  A  #################################################  9800
       B  ################  3100   68% lower
```

Both bars for build B are less than half the length of the bars for build A.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change, B vs A | Do the ranges overlap? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405..418) | 409 (401..415) | -3 (-0.7%) | Yes |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116..121) | 119 (117..121) | +1 (+0.8%) | Yes |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890..2610) | 870 (820..940) | -1270 (-59%) | No |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200..14100) | 3100 (2700..3900) | -6700 (-68%) | No |
| RSS at end of run, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) | Range not recorded |

## What the data shows

- **p99 and p99.9 latency are lower with jf2, by more than the variation between runs.** The slowest build B run is faster than the fastest build A run: 940 us against 1890 us for p99, and 3900 us against 7200 us for p99.9.
- **jf2 results vary less between runs.** The p99 range is 120 us wide for build B and 720 us wide for build A.
- **Throughput and p50 latency show no measurable change.** The differences (3 kops/s and 1 us) are smaller than the range of each build (13 to 14 kops/s and 4 to 5 us).
- **jf2 uses more memory.** RSS at the end of the run is 5.7 GB (9.3%) higher.

## Likely cause

- **Observation in build A:** the latency spikes (short periods of much slower requests) occur at the same times as the decay purge. In the perf profile, 31% of the samples taken during the spike periods are in je_arena_decay.
- **Design difference:** jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- **Hypothesis:** the latency reduction comes from moving the purge to the background thread. A perf profile of build B under the same workload would confirm or reject this.

## One run was repeated

Run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7. The stall was traced to logrotate (the nightly scheduled log clean-up job on the host), not to the allocator. The run was repeated, and the results use the repeat, not the original run.

## Not tested

- ycsb-a (the write-heavy workload).
- More than 64 client threads.
- NUMA pinning.

## Open decision

Is an RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment) behind a feature flag (a configuration switch).

## References

- [Ref1] YCSB core workloads: https://github.com/brianfrankcooper/YCSB/wiki/Core-Workloads

---

**Gaps in the notes (for you, not for the team):**

- **RSS:** the notes give one value per build with no lowest and highest run. I assumed the value is the median of 5 runs, like the other rows.
- **Build B profile:** the notes do not mention a perf profile of build B, so I wrote the cause as a hypothesis.
- **Workload mix:** the 95/5 and 50/50 read/update ratios come from the YCSB documentation, not from your notes. Check them if kestrel uses modified workloads.
- **Date:** "tomorrow" is 2026-11-21, which is a Saturday. Change the date if you meant the next working day.
